title: Electroencephalography (EEG)
path: Management of Clients with Neurologic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction and Principles of Electroencephalography
headings.content: Electroencephalography is a non-invasive diagnostic tool that measures the electrical activity of the brain. Small metallic discs called **electrodes** are placed on the scalp using a conductive paste or gel according to the standardized 10-20 international system. These electrodes detect tiny electrical voltage fluctuations resulting from ionic current flows within the dendrites of the brain's neurons. The recorded signals are amplified thousands of times and displayed on a monitor or paper as a continuous wave tracing called an electroencephalogram. Unlike structural imaging like CT scans or MRIs which show the physical anatomy of the brain, EEG evaluates real-time functional activity and neurological dynamics.

headings.title: Clinical Indications and Diagnostic Uses
headings.content: Medical teams order EEGs to investigate a wide variety of central nervous system disorders. The most common application is the diagnosis, classification, and management of **epilepsy** and seizure disorders. Beyond seizures, the test helps evaluate altered states of consciousness, unexplained encephalopathies, sleep disorders, and brain death confirmation. It is also instrumental in monitoring patients placed in medically induced comas or assessing localized cerebral dysfunction after head trauma. In busy Nigerian teaching hospitals, EEG is frequently requested when patients present with recurrent unexplained fainting spells or sudden behavioral changes that mimic psychiatric illness.

headings.title: Brain Wave Frequencies and Physiological Patterns
headings.content:
Normal brain activity is categorized into distinct frequency bands measured in Hertz (Hz). Recognizing these rhythms helps differentiate normal states of awareness from pathological conditions.

- **Alpha waves**: Frequency of 8 to 13 Hz; prominent in the occipital region when a person is awake, relaxed, and has their eyes closed.
- **Beta waves**: Frequency greater than 13 Hz; associated with active thinking, problem-solving, alertness, or the ingestion of sedative medications.
- **Theta waves**: Frequency of 4 to 7 Hz; normal during sleep in adults or emotional stress, but abnormal in awake adults.
- **Delta waves**: Frequency under 4 Hz; dominant during deep, non-REM sleep in healthy adults and pathologic when present in awake adults.

headings.title: Pre-Procedure Nursing Preparation
headings.content:
Proper preparation ensures diagnostic accuracy and prevents test cancellation. The nurse must provide clear instructions to the client and family members well before the scheduled test time.

- **Hair Hygiene**: Instruct the client to wash their hair thoroughly with shampoo the night before to remove natural oils, sprays, or gels that impede electrode contact. Avoid using conditioners or oils.
- **Sleep Deprivation**: If ordered by the physician for seizure provocation, instruct the client to restrict sleep (e.g., staying awake past midnight or sleeping only 4 hours).
- **Medication Management**: Clarify with the attending physician whether routine anticonvulsants or sedatives should be withheld, as many medications alter brain wave patterns.
- **Dietary Considerations**: Advise the client to eat a normal meal beforehand to prevent hypoglycemia, but restrict caffeine-containing beverages like coffee, tea, and soda for at least 8 to 12 hours.

headings.title: Intra-Procedure Care and Provocative Techniques
headings.content:
During the recording, the client lies comfortably on a bed or recliner. The technician applies a conductive paste and places about 20 electrodes across the scalp regions. The nurse reassures the anxious client, emphasizing that electrodes only record electricity and do not deliver shocks. Throughout the session, standard provocative activation techniques may be used to elicit latent or hidden abnormal electrical discharges.

- **Hyperventilation**: The client breathes deeply and rapidly for about 3 minutes, which induces cerebral vasoconstriction and hypocapnia, frequently triggering absence seizures or spike-wave discharges.
- **Photic Stimulation**: A flashing light stroboscope is placed in front of the client at varying frequencies to test for photosensitive epilepsy.
- **Sleep Induction**: Allowing the client to sleep during the recording helps capture abnormalities that only surface during non-REM stages.

headings.title: Post-Procedure Care and Safety
headings.content: Once the recording concludes, the technologist removes the electrodes and washes away remaining conductive paste using warm water, acetone, or a gentle solvent. The client may experience sticky hair or mild scalp tenderness from the pressure of the application discs. If sleep deprivation or sedative medications were used, the client requires close observation and assistance with ambulation to prevent accidental falls. The nurse ensures that any withheld routine medications, particularly anticonvulsants, are safely re-administered as soon as the test is complete.

headings.title: Interpreting Results and Artifact Management
headings.content: Neurologists and clinical neurophysiologists interpret EEG recordings by analyzing background rhythms, symmetry between hemispheres, and reactivity to stimuli. Abnormal findings include **spike-and-wave discharges**, sharp waves, or focal slowing indicative of structural lesions or focal epilepsy. A major challenge in interpretation is distinguishing true cerebral abnormalities from **artifacts**—non-cerebral electrical signals recorded by the machine. Common artifacts include muscle tension, eye blinking, patient movement, and 50/60 Hz electrical interference from hospital power lines.

headings.title: Limitations and Special Considerations
headings.content: While valuable, EEG has inherent diagnostic limitations. A normal interictal EEG does not completely rule out epilepsy, as many patients with seizure disorders have normal brain wave tracings between active episodes. Conversely, false positives can occur when normal variants mimic epileptiform patterns. Additionally, deep-seated brain lesions located far from the cortical surface may not generate sufficient electrical voltage to be detected by scalp electrodes. Clinical correlation with patient history, witness accounts, and imaging remains vital for accurate diagnosis.
